clue.text: Separate blocks spinning still function

indicators.note: one piece blocks, or sits in the way of, the other, so the separate piece goes inside
spinning turns the word for still round so it reads the other way

parts.note: still, as in 'yet to come', means yet
separate, as an adverb, means apart

explanation.surface: Someone describes an engine or machine part that keeps working even while blocks spin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spinning' turns the word for still round, and 'blocks' sets the separate piece inside it. 'function' looks like a purpose, but here it is a social event.
explanation.definitionFit: A social gathering or occasion is called a function, and an afternoon party with tea is one such event.

clue.text: Bomber rising unaccompanied and not straight

indicators.note: in a down clue, rising means a word is read from the bottom up, so backwards

parts.note: unaccompanied means alone
not straight, meaning not heterosexual, gives gay

explanation.surface: A bomber plane climbs on its own and veers off course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rising' makes ALONE read upwards as ENOLA. The Enola Gay was the B-29 that dropped the atomic bomb on Hiroshima.
explanation.definitionFit: The Enola Gay is a famous named aircraft, the B-29 bomber used over Hiroshima in 1945.

clue.text: Over the phone, correct butcher's misleading information

indicators.note: something said over the phone is heard rather than seen, so what counts is how it sounds

parts.note: correct means proper, and butcher's is rhyming slang for a look (butcher's hook), as is gander

explanation.surface: A phone call complains that a butcher has been spreading false stories.
explanation.walkthrough: PROPER GANDER, said aloud, is the answer. 'Butcher's' is Cockney rhyming slang: butcher's hook means look, and a gander is also a look.
explanation.definitionFit: Propaganda is information, often biased or false, spread to sway public opinion.

clue.text: Wrap painful swelling enveloping boy's foot in game

parts.note: a wrap or blanket is a rug

indicators.note: enveloping means wrapping round, so the boy's last letter goes inside the swelling

parts.note: a painful swelling on the foot is a bunion

indicators.note: in a down clue the foot is the bottom, so the last letter of the word

explanation.surface: Someone bandages a boy's bunion before he plays a match.
explanation.walkthrough: The boy's foot is Y, his last letter, which goes inside BUNION after the B. Rugby union is the fifteen-a-side form of rugby.
explanation.definitionFit: Rugby union is a team sport, the fifteen-a-side version of rugby football.

clue.text: Food unusually tough, and rubbery in the extreme

indicators.note: unusually says the letters are set out in an unusual order
the extremes of a word are its first and last letters

explanation.surface: A diner complains that a dish is oddly tough and rubbery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in the extreme' takes R and Y, the ends of rubbery; 'unusually' rearranges them with TOUGH.
explanation.definitionFit: Yoghurt is a foodstuff, milk fermented with bacteria.

clue.text: Baker's loaves primarily to feed family

definitions.note: Baker's is read as 'baker is': the answer is a thing that bakes, so a baker

indicators.note: something given to feed someone goes into them, so a letter goes inside

parts.note: family means kin

indicators.note: primarily means first, so the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: A baker's bread goes first to feed the family.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a person who makes bread, but the baker here is an oven that fires pottery or bricks.
explanation.definitionFit: A kiln is an oven for firing clay, so it is literally something that bakes.

clue.text: Fleet Street put off celebrity raving over article

indicators.note: put off means taken away, so the letters for street are removed from celebrity

parts.note: a celebrity is a star
raving means mad
a is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: Fleet Street, home of the British newspapers, is upset by a celebrity going wild over a story.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fleet Street' looks like one phrase, the London home of the British press, but it splits: Fleet is the definition and 'put off' removes the street from the celebrity.
explanation.definitionFit: An armada is a fleet of warships, most famously the Spanish one of 1588.

clue.text: System regularly adopted by Treasury men, along with the board

indicators.note: something adopted by a household is taken in, so the letters go inside

parts.note: a treasury, a store of valuables, is a chest

indicators.note: regularly means taking every other letter of the word

explanation.surface: A government system is regularly taken up by Treasury officials and the board.
explanation.walkthrough: 'regularly' picks the odd letters of System, and 'adopted by' sets them in the treasury. 'Treasury men' wants to be civil servants, but men starts the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A chess set is the pieces, called chessmen, together with the board they play on.

clue.text: Goal to mix with rich, powerful businessman

indicators.note: to mix means the letters are stirred together into a new order

explanation.surface: An ambitious man aims to rub shoulders with the rich and powerful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to mix' rearranges GOAL with RICH. The word is associated especially with Russian tycoons.
explanation.definitionFit: An oligarch is one of a small group holding power, now usually a very rich and influential tycoon.

clue.text: Farewell performance by one no good

parts.note: a performance by one person is a solo

explanation.surface: A singer's farewell show is a one-person act and a poor one.
explanation.definitionFit: This phrase is an informal goodbye, an alternative to cheerio.

clue.text: Counters with something to sit on inside

indicators.note: with says one piece is joined to the other, here the counters follow

parts.note: a behind, the backside, is what you sit on
bar counters in pubs are bars

explanation.surface: A shop has counters with stools set inside it.
explanation.walkthrough: Inside is slang for in prison, as is behind bars.
explanation.definitionFit: Being inside is slang for serving time in jail, locked behind the bars of a cell.

clue.text: Most curious split appearing back on shiny metal

indicators.note: in an across clue, put on means placed after, so the turned piece follows the metal

parts.note: AG is the chemical symbol for silver, a shiny metal

indicators.note: appearing back means the word for split is shown backwards

parts.note: split, meaning leave, is go

explanation.surface: Someone wonders why a piece of shiny metal has split.
explanation.walkthrough: 'appearing back' turns the word for split round; across, 'on' places it after the metal. The superlative is loose: agog means eager in the extreme.
explanation.definitionFit: Being agog is being eagerly curious to the highest degree, all eyes and ears for news.

clue.text: This country drops unexpectedly in a second race

parts.note: for a British paper, this country is the UK
drops of water falling are rain

indicators.note: unexpectedly means the letters turn up in a surprising order

explanation.surface: Britain's weather suddenly turns wet in the middle of a second running event.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unexpectedly' rearranges IN A into IAN. 'race' looks like a contest, but here it means a people or nation.
explanation.definitionFit: Race in the sense of a people or nation: the people of Ukraine, taken together.

clue.text: Corners in valleys retaining zero green light

indicators.note: retaining means holding inside, so the valleys hold the other letters

parts.note: glens are narrow Scottish valleys
zero looks like the letter O
the green light, permission to go, is an OK

explanation.surface: Green light glows dimly in the corners of the valleys.
explanation.walkthrough: 'retaining' has the valleys hold both zero and the green light. An inglenook is the corner beside a big open fireplace.
explanation.definitionFit: Inglenooks are the cosy corners or recesses beside a large open fireplace.

clue.text: Needlepoint hem-one you trimmed at the edges, flush

indicators.note: trimmed at the edges means the outer letters of the phrase are cut away and what lies inside is kept

explanation.surface: A needleworker trims the hem of a piece of needlepoint to make it sit flush.
explanation.definitionFit: Flush is informal for having plenty of cash, and this idiom means being rich.

clue.text: Arriving at Heathrow, perhaps after heading off for confinement

indicators.note: heading off means losing the first letter

parts.note: arriving at an airport such as Heathrow, London's main airport, is flying in

explanation.surface: A traveller arrives at Heathrow and is then taken off into custody.
explanation.walkthrough: Lying-in is an old word for the period of confinement after childbirth.
explanation.definitionFit: Confinement is an old term for the time a mother stays in bed around giving birth.

clue.text: Young male hooligan in possession of ecstasy to distribute

parts.note: a young male is a lad

indicators.note: being in possession of something means holding it, so the drug goes inside the hooligan

parts.note: a hooligan is a lout
E is slang for the drug ecstasy

explanation.surface: A young yob caught holding ecstasy pills intends to deal them.
explanation.definitionFit: To ladle out is to give out freely, like serving soup with a ladle.

clue.text: Nice and accommodating old German, briefly one's number one fan

indicators.note: accommodating means giving room to, so the other letters go inside

parts.note: in Nice, the French city, the word for and is et

indicators.note: briefly means the word is cut short by its final letter

parts.note: the Goths were an ancient Germanic people
one's is read as one is, I plus S

explanation.surface: A kindly host in Nice welcomes an old German who is a devoted fan.
explanation.walkthrough: Nice is the French city, so 'Nice and' is French for and; 'briefly' docks the old German, and 'accommodating' takes him and one's inside.
explanation.definitionFit: An egotist is a person whose biggest fan is themselves, so the definition is a witty way to describe self-love.

clue.text: Nightingale's informally recalled as example ——- grand one -— for singing exercises

indicators.note: recalled means called back, so the word is read in reverse

parts.note: Florence Nightingale, called by the short form of her name, gives Flo's
EG, for exempli gratia, means for example
G is short for grand, slang for a thousand pounds
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Florence Nightingale is fondly remembered for her vocal training.
explanation.walkthrough: 'recalled' turns FLOS into SOLF.
explanation.definitionFit: Solfeggi is the plural of solfeggio, a vocal drill sung to do-re-mi syllables.

clue.text: Rather concerned with appearance, runs for one's shiny coat

indicators.note: for means one letter stands in place of another

parts.note: vain means concerned with appearance, and adding -ish makes it rather so
I is one, the Roman numeral
R is the cricket abbreviation for runs

explanation.surface: A vain person who runs chooses a glossy coat.
explanation.walkthrough: VAINISH, a jokey coinage for 'rather vain', has its first I swapped for R.
explanation.definitionFit: Varnish is a clear liquid that dries to a hard, glossy finish on wood.

clue.text: London landmark contains a pub -a medium that's used in networking

indicators.note: contains means holding something inside, so the other letters go within the landmark

parts.note: the Millennium Dome in Greenwich is a London landmark
a pub is an inn
M is the abbreviation for medium, as on clothes labels

explanation.surface: A London landmark houses a pub frequented by a psychic medium.
explanation.walkthrough: 'medium' looks like a psychic or a means of communication, but it is just M. The Dome is the Millennium Dome, now the O2 arena.
explanation.definitionFit: A domain name is the address used to identify a website on the internet, a computer network.

clue.text: Spectator, perhaps, on endless attraction of Brighton winger

parts.note: The Spectator is a magazine, mag for short

indicators.note: endless means without its last letter

parts.note: Brighton, an English seaside resort, is famous for its pier

explanation.surface: A spectator watches a Brighton winger play football.
explanation.walkthrough: 'winger' wants to be a footballer (Brighton have a football team), but it is anything with wings, here a bird.
explanation.definitionFit: A winger is a jocular word for a creature with wings, and the magpie is a black-and-white bird.

clue.text: Like a slippery catch, hard for the blessed fellow to miss!

indicators.note: to miss means to go without, so these letters are taken away

parts.note: steely means hard, like steel
a blessed fellow is a saint, abbreviated ST

explanation.surface: An angler admits a slippery fish is hard for a holy man to miss.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hard' looks like a description of the catch, but it is STEELY. Removing ST, a saint, leaves the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: An eel is a notoriously slippery fish, so this adjective describes a catch that wriggles like one.

clue.text: Size of work-even method of working — has team rowing at first

indicators.note: at first says the rowing team comes before the other pieces

parts.note: a rowing team or boat of eight oarsmen is an eight
e'en is the poetic short form of even
MO, modus operandi, is a method of working

explanation.surface: A rowing team explains its working method for an even stroke.
explanation.walkthrough: Eighteenmo is a book size, the page formed by folding a sheet into eighteen leaves. 'work' here means a book.
explanation.definitionFit: Eighteenmo, also written 18mo, is a printing format for a book, describing its page size.

clue.text: Count beads removed from casing

indicators.note: removed from casing means the outer letters of the word are stripped off

parts.note: pearls are beads, as on a string

explanation.surface: Someone counts beads taken out of a casing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Count' looks like a verb, but it is a noun: a nobleman. An earl is the British equal of a European count.
explanation.definitionFit: An earl is the British rank matching a Continental count.

clue.text: Woman loves to pester husband

parts.note: love is zero in tennis, which looks like O, so loves are two Os
to pester is to nag

explanation.surface: A woman likes to badger her husband.
explanation.definitionFit: Oonagh is an Irish female forename, so it can stand for any woman.

clue.text: Involved in protest, as weapons expert

definitions.meaning: involved in protest means angrily objecting
read literally, someone well versed in arms is up in them

explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means indignant and protesting, and literally read it means knowledgeable about firearms.

clue.text: One year's shift working could make you wobbly

indicators.note: working means the letters are worked into a new arrangement

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one
Y is the abbreviation for year, with the S of the possessive

explanation.surface: A tired worker says a year of shift work would make anyone shaky.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wobbly' looks like unsteady, but in British slang to throw a wobbly is to have a tantrum.
explanation.definitionFit: A wobbly is British slang for a temper tantrum, as is this phrase.
